name: Model 1 (no drift): change in the short rate
prompt: In Model 1 (normally distributed rates, no drift), what is the change in the short rate over a small interval?

variables.meaning: change in the short-term interest rate over the small interval dt (in %)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)
normally distributed random shock with mean 0 and standard deviation sqrt(dt) (0.2887 for one month)

corruptions.why: That is Model 2: it adds a drift term. Model 1 has no drift, so its expected change is zero.
The volatility multiplies the random shock dw, not the time step; sigma*dt would make the change deterministic.
sigma is the basis-point volatility and enters linearly; squaring it gives a variance, not a rate move.

sensitivities.why: A larger positive shock moves the rate up by sigma times the shock.
Higher volatility amplifies the move in whichever direction dw points: up if dw > 0, down if dw < 0.

intuition: No drift: the rate only takes a random shock scaled by volatility, so on average it goes nowhere.

name: Model 1 tree: the two date-1 rates
prompt: In a Model 1 (no-drift) binomial tree, what are the up and down rates one step after today's rate?

variables.meaning: the up-node and down-node short rates at date 1 (each reached with probability 0.5)
current (date-0) short-term rate, in %
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)

corruptions.why: The one-step standard deviation scales with the square root of time: sigma*sqrt(dt), not sigma*dt.
That is the Model 2 node; Model 1 has no drift, so the tree stays centred on r_0.

sensitivities.why: Both nodes are centred on today's rate.
Higher volatility pushes the up node higher and the down node lower (the nodes spread apart).

intuition: Each step is today's rate plus or minus one standard deviation of the per-step shock; with no drift the tree is centred on r_0 and recombines.

name: Model 1 tree: the outer date-2 rates
prompt: In a Model 1 (no-drift) tree, what are the highest and lowest short rates two steps out?

variables.meaning: the up-up and down-down short rates at date 2 (the middle node is r_0 again)
current (date-0) short-term rate, in %
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)

corruptions.why: sqrt(2)*sigma*sqrt(dt) is the standard deviation after two steps, but the outer node is reached by two full up (or down) moves, so it sits 2*sigma*sqrt(dt) away.
Each step moves the rate by sigma*sqrt(dt), not sigma*dt.

sensitivities.why: The whole tree is centred on today's rate.
Higher volatility raises the up-up node and lowers the down-down node.

intuition: Two up moves stack linearly: 2 sigma sqrt(dt) above r_0, while up-then-down lands back exactly on r_0 (the tree recombines).

name: Standard deviation of the rate change per step
prompt: In the normal (no-drift) model, what is the standard deviation of the short-rate change over one step of length dt?

variables.meaning: standard deviation of the rate change over one step (in %; e.g. 0.326% = 32.6 bp per month)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)

corruptions.why: Volatility scales with the square root of time; sigma*dt would shrink a monthly move to sigma/12 instead of sigma/sqrt(12).
That is the variance of the rate change, not its standard deviation.

sensitivities.why: Higher annual volatility means bigger per-step moves.
A longer step accumulates more variance, growing with sqrt(dt).

intuition: Annual vol times square-root-of-time: for one month multiply by sqrt(1/12) = 0.2887.

name: Model 2 (constant drift): change in the short rate
prompt: In Model 2, which adds a constant drift to the normal model, what is the change in the short rate over a small interval?

variables.meaning: change in the short-term interest rate over the small interval dt (in %)
positive constant drift (in % per year), capturing both a risk premium and expected return
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)
normally distributed random shock with mean 0 and standard deviation sqrt(dt) (0.2887 for one month)

corruptions.why: A time-dependent drift is the Ho-Lee model; Model 2's drift is the same constant every step.
The drift is deterministic and scales with time dt; the volatility scales the random shock dw.

sensitivities.why: A larger drift adds lambda*dt to every step.
A larger positive shock raises the rate change.
Up if the shock dw is positive, down if it is negative.

intuition: Model 1 plus a constant upward push each step: the tree shifts up by lambda*dt every period, giving an upward-sloping term structure.

name: Model 2 tree: the two date-1 rates
prompt: In a Model 2 (constant drift) tree, what are the up and down short rates one step after today?

variables.meaning: the up-node and down-node short rates at date 1
current (date-0) short-term rate, in %
constant annual drift (in %)
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)

corruptions.why: The drift accrues linearly with time (lambda*dt); only the volatility scales with sqrt(dt).
Dropping the drift gives the Model 1 node; Model 2 shifts both nodes up by lambda*dt.
The volatility shock per step is sigma*sqrt(dt), not sigma*dt.

sensitivities.why: Both nodes start from today's rate.
A larger drift lifts both nodes by lambda*dt.
Higher volatility raises the up node and lowers the down node.

intuition: Same fork as Model 1, but the whole fork is first lifted by the drift lambda*dt.

name: Model 2 tree: the outer date-2 rates
prompt: In a Model 2 (constant drift) tree, what are the highest and lowest short rates two steps out?

variables.meaning: the up-up and down-down short rates at date 2 (the middle node is r_0 + 2 lambda dt)
current (date-0) short-term rate, in %
constant annual drift (in %)
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)

corruptions.why: The drift accrues every step, so after two steps the tree has shifted by 2*lambda*dt.
Two full up moves put the outer node 2*sigma*sqrt(dt) away; sqrt(2) is the two-step standard deviation, not a node.

sensitivities.why: The tree is built on today's rate.
Each of the two steps adds lambda*dt.
Higher volatility raises the up-up node and lowers the down-down node.

intuition: After two steps the whole tree has risen by 2 lambda dt; the middle node r_0 + 2 lambda dt is single-valued, so Model 2 recombines.

name: Ho-Lee model: change in the short rate
prompt: In the Ho-Lee model, with a drift that can differ each period, what is the change in the short rate over a small interval?

variables.meaning: change in the short-term interest rate over the small interval dt (in %)
the drift for period t (in % per year): a different, calibrated value each period, which can be negative
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)
normally distributed random shock with mean 0 and standard deviation sqrt(dt) (0.2887 for one month)

corruptions.why: A single constant drift is Model 2; Ho-Lee reduces to it only if every lambda_t is equal.
A drift that depends on the current rate is Vasicek (mean reversion), not Ho-Lee.
Ho-Lee changes only the drift term; volatility sigma stays constant.

sensitivities.why: A higher drift for the period adds lambda_t*dt to the change.
A larger positive shock raises the rate change.
Up if the shock dw is positive, down if it is negative.

intuition: Model 2 with a different, market-calibrated drift each period, so the tree can fit any term-structure shape.

name: Ho-Lee tree: the two date-1 rates
prompt: In a Ho-Lee tree, what are the up and down short rates one step after today?

variables.meaning: the up-node and down-node short rates at date 1
current (date-0) short-term rate, in %
the calibrated drift for the first period (in % per year)
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)

corruptions.why: The first step uses the first period's drift lambda_1; lambda_2 applies to the second step.
Drift accrues linearly with time (lambda_1*dt); only the shock scales with sqrt(dt).

sensitivities.why: Both nodes start from today's rate.
A higher first-period drift lifts both date-1 nodes.
Higher volatility raises the up node and lowers the down node.

intuition: Like Model 2's first step, but the drift is this period's own calibrated lambda_1.

name: Ho-Lee tree: the outer date-2 rates
prompt: In a Ho-Lee tree, what are the highest and lowest short rates two steps out?

variables.meaning: the up-up and down-down short rates at date 2 (the middle node is r_0 + (lambda_1 + lambda_2) dt)
current (date-0) short-term rate, in %
calibrated drift for period 1 (in % per year)
calibrated drift for period 2 (in % per year)
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)

corruptions.why: Each step uses its own drift, so the cumulative shift is (lambda_1 + lambda_2) dt, not twice the latest drift. (With lambda_1 = lambda_2 it reduces to Model 2.)
Two full up moves put the outer node 2*sigma*sqrt(dt) away.

sensitivities.why: The first-period drift is carried into every date-2 node.
The second-period drift lifts every date-2 node.
Higher volatility raises the up-up node and lowers the down-down node.

intuition: Drifts accumulate period by period: after two steps the tree has shifted by (lambda_1 + lambda_2) dt, and it still recombines.

name: Vasicek model: change in the short rate
prompt: In the mean-reverting Vasicek model, what is the change in the short rate over a small interval?

variables.meaning: change in the short-term interest rate over the small interval dt (in %)
speed of mean-reversion adjustment (per year); high k means faster mean reversion
long-run value of the short-term rate assuming risk neutrality (in %)
current interest rate level (in %)
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)
normally distributed random shock with mean 0 and standard deviation sqrt(dt) (0.2887 for one month)

corruptions.why: The drift must be positive when the rate is below theta; (r - theta) would push rates away from their long-run level.
k is the speed of reversion: a higher k must mean a faster pull, so it multiplies the gap.
Dropping k removes the speed of reversion: the drift is the gap to theta scaled by k (0.03 in the notes' example), not the full gap.

sensitivities.why: A higher long-run level increases the pull upward.
The further the rate rises toward (or above) theta, the smaller (or more negative) the drift.
Raises dr when r is below theta, lowers it when r is above theta.
A larger positive shock raises the rate change.

intuition: The drift is a rubber band: k times the gap to theta pulls the rate back toward its long-run level.

name: Vasicek: long-run risk-neutral level theta
prompt: In the Vasicek model, how is the risk-neutral long-run rate theta approximated from the true long-run rate, the drift and the reversion speed?

variables.meaning: long-run value of the short-term rate assuming risk neutrality (in %)
the long-run true rate of interest (in %)
the annual drift (in %)
speed of mean-reversion adjustment (per year); high k means faster mean reversion

corruptions.why: The drift is divided by k: slow reversion (small k) lets a small risk premium lift theta a long way (0.36%/0.03 = 12 points).
Theta builds on the long-run true rate r_1, not the current rate r.
A positive drift/risk premium raises the risk-neutral long-run level above the true rate.

sensitivities.why: Theta is the true long-run rate plus an add-on.
A larger drift raises the add-on lambda/k.
Faster reversion shrinks the add-on lambda/k (for positive lambda).

intuition: Risk-neutral long-run level = true long-run rate plus the drift grossed up by 1/k.

name: Vasicek tree: up and down moves

variables.meaning: change in the short-term interest rate over the small interval dt (in %)
speed of mean-reversion adjustment (per year); high k means faster mean reversion
long-run value of the short-term rate assuming risk neutrality (in %)
the rate at the node you are stepping from (in %)
small time interval, in years (one month = 1/12)
annual basis-point volatility of rate changes (in %, e.g. 1.20%)
normally distributed random shock with mean 0 and standard deviation sqrt(dt) (0.2887 for one month)

corruptions.why: The drift is the same on both branches; only the volatility term is added for up moves and subtracted for down moves.
The drift is recomputed at each node's own rate, not frozen at r_0; that is exactly why the two middle nodes differ (6.258% vs 6.260%).
The volatility multiplies the random shock dw (sqrt(dt) per step), not dt.

sensitivities.why: A higher long-run level raises the drift on both branches.
A higher starting node shrinks the drift k(theta - r) on both branches.

name: Vasicek: expected rate in T years (gap-decay form)
prompt: Under Vasicek, what is the expected short rate T years ahead, written as the long-run level minus the decayed gap?

variables.meaning: expected short rate in T years (in %)
the long-run mean-reverting level (in %)
the current short-term rate (in %)
the speed of mean reversion (per year)
the horizon, in years

corruptions.why: The gap must decay, so the exponent is negative; e^{kT} makes the gap grow.
That is only the remaining gap (8.74% in the notes' example); the expected rate is theta minus that gap (9.26%).
Starting below theta, the rate approaches theta from below; adding the gap would put it above theta.

sensitivities.why: The expected rate is pulled toward theta, with weight 1 - e^{-kT}.
Today's rate still carries weight e^{-kT}.
Faster reversion moves the expectation closer to theta: up if r_0 < theta, down if r_0 > theta.
A longer horizon moves the expectation closer to theta: up if r_0 < theta, down if r_0 > theta.

intuition: Take the gap to the long-run level, shrink it by e^{-kT}, and subtract what is left from theta.

name: Vasicek: expected rate in T years (weighted-average form)
prompt: Under Vasicek, write the expected short rate T years ahead as a weighted average of today's rate and the long-run level.

variables.meaning: expected short rate in T years (in %)
the current short-term rate (in %)
the long-run mean-reverting level (in %)
the speed of mean reversion (per year)
the horizon, in years

corruptions.why: The weights are swapped: as T grows the weight on today's rate (e^{-kT}) must vanish, leaving theta.
The exponent must be negative so that today's rate's weight decays over time.

sensitivities.why: Today's rate carries weight e^{-kT} > 0.
The long-run level carries weight 1 - e^{-kT} > 0.
Shifts weight from r_0 to theta: up if r_0 < theta, down if r_0 > theta.

intuition: A blend of today's rate and the long-run level; the weight on today decays as e^{-kT}.

calc.expr: r0 * Math.exp(-k * T) + theta * (1 - Math.exp(-k * T))

name: Vasicek half-life
prompt: Under Vasicek, how long does it take for the gap between the current rate and the long-run mean to halve?

variables.meaning: half-life, in years: the time for the gap between the current rate and the long-run mean to be halved
the speed of mean reversion (per year)

corruptions.why: Faster reversion (higher k) must shorten the half-life, so k belongs in the denominator.
The gap decays exponentially, e^{-k tau} = 1/2, so the constant is ln(2) = 0.6931, not 0.5.

sensitivities.why: A stronger pull toward theta halves the gap faster.

intuition: 0.693 divided by the reversion speed; it does not depend on how big the gap is (k = 0.03 gives about 23.1 years).

name: Backtest failure rate

number of exceptions
number of samples (observations in the backtest window)

The same exceptions over more days is a lower rate.

intuition: Exceptions divided by days; if it is well above 1 - confidence (1% for 99% VaR), the model underestimates risk.

name: Normal-approximation z-test on exceptions

variables.meaning: test statistic; reject the model if |z| exceeds the critical value (1.96 at 95% two-tailed in the notes' example)
observed number of exceptions
tail probability implied by the confidence level (decimal, e.g. 0.05 for 95% VaR)
number of observations

corruptions.why: The denominator is the standard deviation of the count, sqrt(p(1-p)T), not its variance.
The binomial count's variance is p(1-p)T; dropping T mis-scales the statistic.
Compare the observed count with the expected count pT, not with the probability p.

sensitivities.why: More observed exceptions push z further above zero.
For a fixed count, more days raise the expected count pT faster than the standard error grows.

intuition: (Observed - expected exceptions) divided by the binomial standard deviation; beyond 1.96, reject the model.

name: Kupiec unconditional coverage log-likelihood ratio

variables.meaning: unconditional coverage test statistic; reject the model if LR > 3.841
tail probability implied by the confidence level (decimal)
number of exceptions
number of observations
the observed failure rate

corruptions.why: The signs are flipped, which makes the statistic negative; the log-likelihood under the observed rate is the larger one, so -2 goes on the model's (p) term.
p is the exception probability, so it is raised to the number of exceptions N and (1 - p) to the T - N non-exceptions.

sensitivities.why: The statistic grows as the observed rate N/T moves away from p in either direction; it is zero when N/T = p.

intuition: Compares the likelihood of the data at the model's p with that at the observed rate N/T; the further apart, the bigger LR, and above 3.841 reject.

More clustering adds to the combined statistic.

intuition: Right number of exceptions plus not clustered; the sum is judged against 5.99, each part against 3.84.
